nodes.name: Simple Ring
nodes.statement: A ring $R$ is simple if the only two-sided-ideals of $R$ are ${0}$ and $R$. An algebra is simple if it is simple as a ring.
Division rings are simple.
Let $A$ be a simple ring, then centre of $A$ is a field.
nodes.label: lem:center-simple-ring

nodes.statement: Let $0\ne x$ be an element of centre of $A$. Then $I := \{xy | y\in A\}$ is a two-sided-ideal of $A$. Since $0\ne x\in I$, we have that $I = A$. Therefore $1 \in I$, hence $x$ is invertible.

nodes.name: Central Algebras
nodes.statement: Let $R$ be a ring and $A$ an $R$-algebra, we say $A$ is central if and only if the centre of $A$ is $R$
Every commutative ring is a central algebra over itself.
Simpleness is invariant under ring isomorphism and centrality is invariant under algebra isomorphism.
If $A$ is a central $R$-algerba, $A^{\mathsf{opp}}$ is also central. .
nodes.label: lem:opp-central

nodes.statement: $R$ is a simple ring if and only if any ring homomorphism $f : R \to S$ either injective or $S$ is the trivial ring.
nodes.label: lem:simple-ring-iff

nodes.statement: If $R$ is simple, then the $\ker f$ is either $\{0\}$ or $R$. The former case implies that $f$ is injective while the latter case implies that $S$ is the trivial ring. Conversely, let $I\subseteq R$ be a two-sided-ideal. Consider $\pi: R \to {}^{R}/_{I}$, either $\pi$ is injective implying that $I = \{0\}$ or that ${}^{R}/_{I}$ is the trivial ring implying that $I = R$.
If $A$ is a simple $R$-algebra, ``ring homomorphism'' in \cref{lem:simple-ring-iff} can be replaced with $R$-algebra homomorphism.
Assume $R$ is a field. Let $A, B$ be finite dimensional $R$-algebras where $A$ is simple as well. Then any $R$-algebra homomorphism $f:A\to B$ is bijective if $\dim_{R}A=\dim_{R}B$.
nodes.label: cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:simple-ring-iff}, $f$is injective. Then $\dim_{K}\mathrm{im} f = \dim_{K} B - \dim_{K}\ker f = \dim_{K}B$ meaning that $f$ is surjective.
If $A$ and $B$ are central $K$-algebras, $A\otimes_{K}B$ is a central $K$-algebra as well.
nodes.label: lem:tensor-central

nodes.statement: Assume $A$ and $B$ are central algebras, then by~\cref{cor:center-tensor-center} $Z\left(A\otimes_{R}B\right)=Z\left(A\right)\otimes_{R}Z\left(B\right)=R\otimes_{R}R=R$.
If $A$ is a simple $K$-algebra and $B$ is a central simple $K$-algebra, $A\otimes_{K}B$ is a central simple $K$-algebra as well.
nodes.label: thm:tensor-csa

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:tensor-central}, we need to prove $A\otimes_{K}B$ is a simple ring. Denote $f$ as the map $A\to A\otimes_{K}B$. It is sufficient to prove that for every two-sided-ideal $I\subseteq A\otimes_{K}B$, we have $I = \left\langle f\left(f^{-1}\left(I\right)\right)\right\rangle$. Indeed, since $A$ is simple $f^{-1}\left(I\right)$ is either $\left\{0\right\}$ or $A$, if it is $\left\{0\right\}$, then $I=\left\{0\right\}$; if it is $A$, then $I$ is $A$ as well. We will prove that $I \le \left\langle f\left(f^{-1}\left(I\right)\right)\right\rangle$, the other direction is straightforward. Without loss of generality assume $I\ne\left\{0\right\}$. Let $\mathcal{A}$ be an arbitrary basis of $A$, by \cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we see that every element $x \in A\otimes_{K}B$ can be written as $\sum_{i=0}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}\otimes b_{i}$ for some natrual number $n$ and some choice of $b_{i}\in B$ and $\mathcal{A}_{i}\in \mathcal{A}$. Since $I$ is not empty, we see there exists a non-zero element $\omega\in I$ such that its expansion $\sum_{i=0}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}\otimes b_{i}$ has the minimal $n$. In particular, all $b_{i}$ are non-zero and $n\ne0$. We have $\omega=\mathcal{A}_{0}\otimes b_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}\otimes b_{i}$. Since $B$ is simple, $1 \in B = \left\langle\langle b_{0} \right\rangle$; hence we write $1\in\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{i}b_{0}y_{i}$ for some $x_{i},y_{i}\in B$. Define $\Omega := \sum_{j=0}^{m}(1\otimes x_{i})\omega(1\otimes y_{i})$ which is also in $I$. We write \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \mathcal{A}_{0} \otimes \left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{0}y_{j}\right) + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\right) \\ &= \mathcal{A}_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\right) \end{aligned} \] For every $\beta\in B$, we have that $\left(1\otimes \beta\right)\Omega - \Omega\left(1\otimes \beta\right)$ is in I and is equal to \[ \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\beta x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}-x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\beta\right), \] which is an expansion of $n-1$ terms, thus $\left(1\otimes\beta\right)\Omega-\Omega\left(1\otimes\beta\right)$ must be $0$. Hence we conclude that for all $i=1,\dots,n$, $\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}\in Z\left(B\right)=K$. Hence for all $i=1,\dots,n$, we find a $\kappa_{i}\in K$ such that $\kappa_{i}=\sum_{j=0}^{m}x_{j}b_{i}y_{j}$. Hence we can calculate $\Omega$ as \[ \begin{aligned} \Omega &= \mathcal{A}_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}\otimes\left(\sum_{j=0}^{m}\right) \\ &= \mathcal{A}_{0}\otimes 1 + \sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathcal{A}_{i}\otimes\kappa_{i} \\ &= \left(\mathcal{A}_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot\mathcal{A}_{i}\right) \otimes 1 \end{aligned}. \] From this, we note that $\mathcal{A}_{0}+\sum_{i}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot\mathcal{A}_{i}\in f^{-1}\left(I\right)$; since $A$ is simple, we immediately conclude that $f^{-1}\left(I\right) = A$, once we know $\mathcal{A}_{0}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\kappa_{i}\cdot \mathcal{A}_{i}$ is not zero. If it is zero, by the fact that $\mathcal{A}$ is a linearly independent set, we conclude that $1,\kappa_{1},\dots,\kappa_{n}$ are all zero; which is a contradiction. Since $f^{-1}\left(I\right) = A$, we know $\left\langle f\left(f^{-1}I\right)\right\rangle = A \otimes_{K} B$.
Central simple algebras are stable under base change. That is, if $L/K$ is a field extension and $D$ is a central simple algebra over $K$, then $L\otimes_{K} D$ is central simple over $L$.
nodes.label: cor:csa-basechange

nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $L\otimes_{K} D$ is simple. Let $x\in Z\left(L\otimes_{K}D\right)$, by~\cref{cor:center-tensor-center}, we have $x\in Z\left(L\right)\otimes Z\left(D\right)=Z\left(L\right)$. Without loss of generality, we can assume that $x = l \otimes d$ is a pure tensor, then $l \in Z\left(L\right)$ and $d \in K$. Therefore $x = d\cdot l \in L$.
If $A\otimes_{K} B$ is a simple ring, then $A$ and $B$ are both simple.
nodes.label: thm:tensor-simple-implies-simple

nodes.statement: By symmetry, we only prove that $A$ is simple. If $A$ or $B$ is the trivial ring then $A\otimes_{K} B$ is the trivial ring, a contradiction. Thus we assume both $A$ and $B$ are non-trivial. Suppose $A$ is not simple, by~\cref{lem:simple-ring-iff}, there exists a non-trivial $K$-algebra $A'$ and a $K$-algebra homomorphism $f : A \to A'$ such that $\ker f \not= \{0\}$. Let $F : A \otimes_{K} B\to A'\otimes_{K} B$ be the base change of $f$, then since $A\otimes_{K} B$ is simple and $A'\otimes B$ is non-trivial ($A'$ is non-trivial and $B$ is faithfully flat because $B$ is free), we conclude that $F$ is injective. Then we have that \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} 0 \arrow{r}{0} & A \otimes_{K} B \arrow{r}{F} & A'\otimes_K B \end{tikzcd} \end{center} is exact. Since $B$ is faithfully flat as a $K$-module, tensorig with $B$ reflects exact sequences, therefore \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} 0 \arrow{r}{0} & A \arrow{r}{f} & A' \end{tikzcd} \end{center} is exact as well. This is contradiction since $f$ is not injective.

nodes.name: Subfield
nodes.statement: For any field $K$ and $K$-algebra $A$, a subfield $B \subseteq A$ is a commutative $K$-subalgebra of $A$ that is closed under inverse for any non-zero member.
Subfields inherit a natural ordering from subalgebras.
Let $k$ be a maximal subfield of $D$, \[ \dim_{K}D = {\left(\dim_{K}k\right)}^{2}. \]
nodes.label: lem:dim-maximal-subfield

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, we have that $\dim_{K} D = \dim_{K}C_{D}(k)\cdot \dim_{K}k$. Hence it is sufficient to show that $C_{D}(k) = k$. By the commutativity of $k$, we have that $k \le C_{D}(k)$. Suppose $k \ne C_{D}(k)$: let $a \in C_{D}(k)$ that is not in $k$. We see that $L := k(a)$ is another subalgebra of $D$ that is strictly larger than $k$; a contradiction. Therefore $k = C_{D}(k)$ and the theorem is proved.

Suppose $L$ is a subfield of $A$, the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item $L$ = $C_{A}(L)$ \item $\dim_{K}A = {\left(\dim_{K}L\right)}^{2}$ \item for any commutative $K$-subalgebra $L' \subseteq A$, $L \subseteq L'$ implies $L = L'$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: lem:tfae-subfield

nodes.statement: We prove the following: \begin{itemize} \item ``1. implies 2.'': this is~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}. \item ``2. implies 1.'': Since $L$ is commutative, we always have $L \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. Hence we only need to show $\dim_{K}L = \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)$. This is because by~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, we have that $\dim_{K}A = \dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)$ and by 2. we have $\dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}C_{A}(L)= \dim_{K}L\cdot \dim_{K}L$. \item ``2. implies 3.'': Since 2. implies 1., we assume $L = C_{A}(L)$, therefore all we need is to prove $L' \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. Let $x \in L'$ and $y \in L \subseteq L'$, we need to show $xy = yx$ which is commutativity of $L'$. \item ``3. implies 1.'': By commutativity of $L$, we always have $L \subseteq C_{A}(L)$. For the other direction, suppose $C_{A}(L)\not\subseteq L$, then there exists some $a \in C_{A}(L)$ but not in $L$. Consider $L' = L(a)$, by 3., we have $L' = L$ which is a contradiction. \end{itemize}

Note that all modules are assumed to be left modules; when we need to consider right $R$-modules, we will consider left $R^{\mathsf{opp}}$-modules instead. We use $\delta_{ij}$ to denote the matrix whose $(i,j)$-th entry is $1$ and $0$ elsewhere. $\delta_{ij}$ forms a basis for matrices.

nodes.name: Morita Equivalence
nodes.statement: The functors constructed in \cref{con:morita-eqv-functor0} and \cref{con:morita-eqv-functor1} form an equivalence of category.
nodes.label: thm:morita

nodes.statement: Let $M$ be an $R$-module, then the unit $\widetilde{\widehat{M}} \cong M$ is given by \[ \begin{aligned} x \mapsto \sum_{j} x_{j} \\ (x,0,\dots,0) \mapsfrom x \end{aligned} \] Let $M$ be an $\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(R)$-module, then the counit $\widehat{\widetilde{M}}\cong M$ is given by $m \mapsto (\delta_{i0}\cdot m)$. This map is both injective and surjective.
Let $M$ and $N$ be simple $A$-modules, then $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic as $A$-modules.
nodes.label: lem:isomorphic-simple-mod

nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, there exists non-zero $n\in\mathbb N$, $k$-division algebra $D$ such that $A\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$ as $k$-algebras. Then by~\cref{thm:morita}, we have equivalence of category $e : \mathfrak{Mod}_{A}\cong\mathfrak{Mod}_{D}$. Since simple module is a categorical notion (it can be defined in terms monomorphisms), $e(M)$ and $e(N)$ are simple $D$-modules. Since $D$ is a division ring, $e(M)$ and $e(N)$ are isomorphic as $D$-modules, therefore $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic as $A$-modules.
Let $M$ be an $A$-module, there exists a simple $A$-module $S$ such that $M$ is a direct sum of copies of $S$, i.e. $M \cong \bigoplus_{i \in \iota} S$ for some indexing set $\iota$.
nodes.label: lem:direct-sum-simple-mod

nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, there exists non-zero $n\in\mathbb N$, $k$-division algebra $D$ such that $A\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$ as $k$-algebras. Then by~\cref{thm:morita}, we have equivalence of category $e : \mathfrak{Mod}_{A}\cong\mathfrak{Mod}_{D}$. Since simple module is a categorical notion (it can be defined in terms monomorphisms), $e^{-1}(D)$ is a simple module over $A$. Since $e(M)$ is a free module over $D$, we can write $e(M)$ as $\bigoplus_{i\in \iota} D$ for some indexing set $\iota$. By precomposing the unit of $e$, we get an isomorphism $M \cong e^{-1}\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\iota} D\right)$. We only need to prove $e^{-1}\left(\bigoplus_{i\in\iota} D\right)\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}e^{-1}\left(D\right)$. This is because direct sum is the categorical coproduct.

Note that by~\cref{lem:isomorphic-simple-mod}, any two simple $A$-module are isomorphic, hence for any $A$-module $M$ and {\em any} simple $A$-module $S$, we can write $M$ as a direct sum of copies of $S$.
Let $M$ and $N$ be two finite $A$-module with compatible $k$-action. Then $M$ and $N$ are isomorphic as $A$-module if and only if $\dim_{k} M$ and $\dim_{k} N$ are equal.
nodes.label: lem:iso-of-dim-eq

nodes.statement: The forward direction is trivial as an $A$-linear isomorphism is a $k$-linear isomorphism as well. Conversely, suppose $\dim_{k}M = \dim_{k}N$. By~\cref{lem:direct-sum-simple-mod}, there exists a simple $A$-module $S$ such that $M \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} S$ and $N \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota'} S$ as $A$-modules. Without loss of generality $S \ne 0$, for otherwise we have $M \cong N$ anyway. If either of $\iota$ or $\iota'$ is empty, then $\dim_{k}M = \dim_{k} N = 0$ implying that $M = N = 0$, we again have $M \cong N$. Thus, we assume both $\iota$ and $\iota'$ are non-empty. By pulling back the $A$-module structure on $S$ to a $k$-module structure along $k \hookrightarrow A$, $M, N, S, \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} S, \bigoplus_{i\in\iota'} S$ are all finite dimensional $k$-vector spaces. Hence $\iota$ and $\iota'$ are finite. The equality $\dim_{k}M=\dim_{k}N$ tells us that $\iota \cong \iota'$ as set, hence $M \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota}S\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota'}S\cong N$ as required.
$D^{n}$ is a simple $A$-module where the module structure is given by pulling back the $\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$-module structure of $D^{n}$.
nodes.label: lem:exists-simple-mod

nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:morita}, we have $\mathfrak{Mod}_{A}\cong\mathfrak{Mod}_{D}\cong\mathfrak{Mod}_{\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)}$. Since $D$ is a simple $D$-module, $D^{n}$ is a simple $\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$ module and consequently, a simple $A$-module.

Note that any $A$-linear endomorphism of $D^{n}$ is $\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$-linear, and vice versa. Thus we have $\mathrm{End}_{A}\left(D^{n}\right)\cong \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)}\left(D^{n}\right)$ as $k$-algebras.
$\mathrm{End}_{A}\left(D^{n}\right)$ is isomorphic to $D^{\mathsf{opp}}$ as $k$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:end-vec-iso

nodes.statement: Indeed, we calculate: \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{End}_{A}\left(D^{n}\right) &\cong \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)}\left(D^{n}\right) & \\ &\cong \mathrm{End}_{D}D & \text{by~\cref{thm:morita},}~\mathfrak{Mod}_{D}\cong\mathfrak{Mod}_{\mathrm{Mat}_{n}D}\\ &\cong D^{\mathsf{opp}} \end{aligned} \]
Let $M$ be a simple $A$-module, then $\mathrm{End}_{A} M\cong D^{\mathsf{opp}}$ as $k$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:end-simple-iso

nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:morita}, $D^{n}$ is simple as $A$-module; hence by~\cref{lem:isomorphic-simple-mod}, $D^{n}$ and $M$ are isomorphic as $A$-module. \Cref{lem:end-vec-iso} gives the desired result.
In particular, if $M$ is a simple $A$-module, then $\mathrm{End}_{A}M$ is a simple $k$-algbera.
Let $M$ be a simple $A$-module, then $\mathrm{End}_{A}M$ has finite $k$-dimension.

By~\cref{thm:wed}, such $D$ and $n$ always exists. Hence we only need to show $D^{\mathsf{opp}}$ has finite $k$-dimension. Since $\dim_{k}A=\dim_{k}\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$ are both finite, we conclude $D^{\mathsf{opp}}$ is finite as a $k$-vector space by pulling back the finiteness along $D \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$.

Note that for all $A$-module $M$, $\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$ is a $k$-algebra as well, with $k \hookrightarrow \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$ given by $a \mapsto (x \mapsto a\cdot x)$. Thus, we always have a $k$-algebra homomorphism $A \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$ given by the $A$-action on $M$. When $A$ is a simple ring, this map is injective.

nodes.name: Balanced Module
nodes.statement: For any ring $A$ and $A$-module $M$, we say $M$ is a balanced $A$-module, if the $A$-linear map $A \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$ is surjective.
nodes.label: def:balanced-mod

nodes.statement: Balancedness is invariant under linear isomorphism.
For any ring $A$, $A$ is balanced as $A$-module.
nodes.label: lem:balanced-self

nodes.statement: If $f \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}A$, then the image of $f(1)$ under $A \to\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}}A$ is $f$ again.
Any simple $A$-module is balanced.

Indeed, if $M$ is a simple $A$-module, then $A \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota} M$ for some indexing set $\iota$ by~\cref{lem:direct-sum-simple-mod}. Since $A$ is balanced, $\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}M$ is balanced. Let $g \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$, we can define a corresponding $G \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{\bigoplus_{i}M}}\left(\bigoplus_{i}M\right)$ by sending $(v_{i})$ to $(g(v_{i}))$. Since $\bigoplus_{i}M$ is balanced, we know that for some $a\in A$, $G$ is the image of $a$ under $A \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{\bigoplus_{i}M}}\left(\bigoplus_{i}M\right)$. Then the image of $a$ under $A \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$ is $g$.
For any simple $A$-module $M$, we have $A \cong \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$ as $k$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:iso-end-end

nodes.statement: The canonical map $A \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$ is both injective and surjective, as $M$ is a balanced $A$-module and $A$ is a simple ring.

Let $M$ and $N$ be $R$-modules such that $\mathcal{C}_{i\in\iota}$ is a basis for $N$, then every elements of $x \in M \otimes_{R} N$ can be uniquely written as $\sum_{i\in\iota}m_{i}\otimes \mathcal{C}_{i}$ where only finitely many $m_{i}$'s are non-zero
nodes.label: lem:expand-tensor-in-basis

nodes.statement: Given the basis $\mathcal{C}$, we have $R$-linear isomorphism $N \cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}R$, hence $M\otimes_{R}N \cong \bigoplus_{i\in\iota}(M\otimes_{R}R)\cong\bigoplus_{i\in\iota}M$ as $R$-modules.

Let $K$ be a field, $M$ and $N$ be flat $K$-modules. Suppose $p \subseteq M$ and $q \subseteq N$ are $K$-submodules, then $(p \otimes_{K} N) \sqcap (M \otimes_{K} q) = p \otimes_{K} q$ as $K$-submodules.
nodes.label: lem:submodule-tensor-submodule

nodes.statement: The hard direction is to show $(p \otimes_{R} N) \sqcap (M \otimes_{R} q) \le p \otimes_{R} q$. Consider the following diagram: \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} p \otimes_{K} q \ar[r, "u"] \ar[d, "\alpha"] & M \otimes_{K} q \ar[r, "v"] \ar[d, "\beta"] & {}^{M}/_{p} \otimes_{K} q \ar[d, "\gamma"] \\ p \otimes_{K} N \ar[r, "u'"] & M \otimes_{K} N \ar[r, "v'"] & ^{M}/_{p} \otimes_{K} N \end{tikzcd} \end{center} Since $^{M}/_{p}$ is flat, $\gamma$ is injective. Let $z \in (p \otimes_{R} N) \sqcap (M \otimes_{R} q) = \mathrm{im} \beta \sqcap \mathrm{im} u'$. By abusing notation, replace $z$ with some elements of $M \otimes_{K} q$ and continue with $\beta(z)\in\mathrm{im} \beta \sqcap \mathrm{im} u'$. Since $v'(\beta(z))=\gamma(v(z))$ and that $\beta(z)\in \mathrm{im} u'$, we conclude that $\gamma(v(z))=0$, that is $z\in\ker v=\mathrm{im} u$. We abuse notation again, let $z \in p \otimes_{K} q$, we need to show $\beta(u(z))\in\mathrm{im} \beta \sqcap \mathrm{im} u'$, but $\beta\circ u=u'\circ\alpha$, we finish the proof.
Let $S, T$ be two subalgebras of $A$, then $C_{A}(S\sqcup T)=C_{A}(S)\sqcap C_{A}(T)$.
nodes.label: lem:sup-centralizer

nodes.statement: If we assume $B$ is free as $R$-module, then for any $R$-subalgebra $S$, we have that $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\mathrm{im}\left(S\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$ is $C_{A}(S) \otimes_{R} B$
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-inclusion-tensor

nodes.statement: Let $w\in C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\mathrm{im}\left(S\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$. Since $B$ is free, we choose an arbitrary basis $\mathcal{B}$; by~\cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we write $w = \sum_{i}m_{i}\otimes_{K}\mathcal{B}_{i}$. It is sufficient to show that $m_{i}\in C_{A}(S)$ for all $i$. Let $a \in S$, we need to show that $m_{i}\cdot a = a \cdot m_{i}$. Since $w$ is in the centralizer, $w \cdot (a\otimes 1) = (a\otimes 1)\cdot w$. Hence we have $\sum_{i}(a\cdot m_{i})\otimes\mathcal{B}_{i}=\sum_{i}(m_{i}\cdot a)\otimes\mathcal{B}_{i}$. By the uniqueness of~\cref{lem:expand-tensor-in-basis}, we conclude $a\cdot m_{i}=m_{i}\cdot a$.

A useful special case is when $S=A$, then since $C_{A}(A)=Z(A)$, we have $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\mathrm{im}\left(A\to A\otimes_{R} B\right)\right)$ is equal to $Z(A)\otimes_{R} B$. Since $\mathrm{im}\left(R\otimes_{R}B\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)=\mathrm{im}\left(A\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)$, we conclude its centralizer in $A\otimes_{R}B$ is $Z(A)\otimes_{R}B$.
Assume $R$ is a field. Let $S$ and $T$ be $R$-subalgebras of $A$ and $B$ respectively. Then $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(S\otimes_{R}T\right)$ is equal to $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R}C_{B}(T)$
nodes.label: cor:centralizer-tensor-centralizer

nodes.statement: From~\cref{lem:submodule-tensor-submodule}, $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R}C_{B}(T)$ is equal to $\left(C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R} B\right)\sqcap \left(A\otimes_{R}C_{B}(T)\right)$. The left hand side $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{R} B$ is equal to $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\mathrm{im}\left(S\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$ and the right hand side is equal to $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\mathrm{im}\left(T\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)$. Hence by~\cref{lem:sup-centralizer}, their intersection is equal to \[C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(\mathrm{im}\left(S\to A\otimes_{R} B\right)\sqcup \mathrm{im}\left(T\to A\otimes_{R}B\right)\right)\] This is precisely $C_{A\otimes_{R}B}\left(S\otimes_{R}T\right)$.
Assume $R$ is a field. The centre of $A\otimes_{R} B$ is $Z\left(A\right)\otimes_{R}Z\left(B\right)$.
nodes.label: cor:center-tensor-center

nodes.statement: Special case of~\cref{cor:centralizer-tensor-centralizer}.

nodes.name: minimal ideal of simple rings
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a ring and $I$ a non-trivial minimal left ideal of $A$, then $I$ is a simple $A$-module.
nodes.label: lemma:min-ideal-simple-ring

nodes.statement: Let $J\le I$ be an $A$-submodule of $I$, suppose $J$ is non-trivial, we prove that $J=I$. Then the image $J'$ of $J$ under $I \hookrightarrow A$ is a non-trivial left ideal of $A$. Since $I \hookrightarrow A$ is injective, it is sufficient to prove that $J' = I$. This is because $J'\le I$ and $J' \not< J$.
Let $A$ be a simple ring and $I$ a non-trivial left ideal. One can write $1 \in A$ as $\sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$ for some $x_{i}\in I$ and $y_{i} \in A$.

Let $I'$ be the two-sided ideal spanned by $I$. Then since $A$ is a simple ring, $I' = A$. Thus $1 \in I'$. One can write $1 \in A$ as $\sum_{i}a_{i}x_{i}b_{i}$ for some $x_{i}\in I$ and $a_{i},b_{i}\in A$, since $I$ is a left ideal $a_{i}x_{i}\in I$ as well.
The $n$, $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ are all non-zero.

If $n$ is $0$, then $1 = 0$ in $A$, but all simple rings are non-trivial. We argue by contradiction to prove that all $x_{i}$ and $y_{i}$ are non-zero. Assume there exists a $j$ such that $y_{j}\ne0$ implies $x_{j} = 0$. Without loss of generality, we assume $j = 0$. Then $1 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$. This contradicts the minimality of $n$.

nodes.name: Wedderburn
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a simple ring and $I$ a non-trivial minimal left ideal. Then there exists a non-zero $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-modules.
nodes.label: thm:wed

nodes.statement: We continue to write $1 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}$ in the shortest possible manner. Then we can define an $A$-linear map $g : I^{n}\to A$ by $(v_{i})\mapsto \sum v_{i}y_{i}$. Then $g$ is surjective: if $a \in A$, then $(ax_{i})$ is mapped to $a$ under $g$. $g$ is injective as well: support $g(v_{i})=0=\sum_{i}v_{i}y_{i}$ with $(v_{i})$ not all zero. Without loss of generality, we assume $v_{0} \ne 0$, then the ideal $\langle v_{0}\rangle$ is equal to $I$ (since $I$ is simple\cref{lemma:min-ideal-simple-ring}). Thus $x_{0}\in I = \langle v_{0}\rangle$; implying that $x_{0}=r\cdot v_{0}$ for some $r\in A$. Thus $1=1 - r\cdot 0 = \sum_{i=0}^{n}x_{i}y_{i}-\sum_{i=0}^{n}r\cdot v_{i}y_{i}$. In this way, we cancelled the term at $i=0$, contradicting the minimality of $n$. Hence $g$ is an isomorphism.

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin (Ideal)
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be an Artinian simple ring. There exists a non-zero $n$ and an ideal $I \subseteq A$ such that $I$ is simple as an $A$-module and $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-module.
nodes.label: thm:wed-artin-ideal

nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed}, we only need a minimal left ideal. Since $A$ is Artinian, such ideal exists.

nodes.name: Wedderburn-Artin (Algebra)
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be a field and $B$ an finite dimensional simple algebra over $K$. There exists a non-zero $n\in\mathbb{N}$ and a division $K$-algebra $S$ such that $B \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(S)$.
nodes.label: thm:wed-artin-algebra

nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-ideal}, we can find a $n$ and a minimal left ideal $I$ such $A \cong I^{n}$ as $A$-modules. Note that ${\left(\mathrm{End}_{B}I\right)}^{\mathsf{opp}}$ is a division ring. Then since $B^{\mathsf{opp}}\cong\mathrm{End}_{B}B\cong{\mathrm{End}_{B}(I^{n})}\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{n}\left(\mathrm{End}_{B}I\right)$ as rings where the final isomorphism is from~\cref{con:end-vec-iso-matrix}, we have $e : B\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}\left(\mathrm{End}_{B}I\right)^{\mathsf{opp}}$ as rings. We also have a $K$-algebra structure on ${\left(\mathrm{End}_{B} I\right)}^{\mathsf{opp}}$ given by $(a \cdot f)(x)=f(a\cdot x)$, and this algebra structure promotes the ring isomorphism $e$ to a $k$-algebra isomorphism.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of Wedderburn-Artin theorem
nodes.statement: Let $B$ be a finite-dimensional simple $K$-algebra. Suppose $B$ is isomorphic as $k$-algebras to both $\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$ and $\mathrm{Mat}_{n'}(D')$ where $n, n'$ are non-zero natural numbers and $D, D'$ are $k$-division algebra, then $n = n'$ and $D \cong D'$ as $k$-algebras.
nodes.label: thm:wed-artin-uniq

nodes.statement: Since $D^{n}$ is a simple $B$-module, by~\cref{lem:end-simple-iso}, we see that $\mathrm{End}_{A}D^{n}\cong D^{\mathsf{opp}}$ and $\mathrm{End}_{A}D^{n}\cong D'^{\mathsf{opp}}$ as $k$-algebras. Thus $D^{\mathsf{opp}}\cong D'^{\mathsf{opp}}$ as $k$-algebras, consequently $D\cong D'$ as $k$-algebras as well. Since $A \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n'}(D')\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n'}(D)$ as $k$-algebras and $A$ is finite $k$-dimensional, a dimension argument shows that $n=n'$.
Let $f : B \to A$ be a $K$-algebra homomorphism, $M^{f}$ is finitely generated as a $B\otimes_{K}\mathrm{End}_{A}M$-module.

Since $M$ is a finite $A$-module and $A$ a finite dimensional $K$-vector space, $M$ is a finite dimensional $K$-vector space as well. Suppose $S \subseteq M$ generates $M$ as $K$-module, the claim is that $S$ generates $M^{f}$ as well. Let $x \in M^{f}$, we write $x = \sum_{i}\lambda_{i}\cdot s_{i}$ with $\lambda_{i}\in K$ and $s_{i}\in S$. Note that $\lambda_{i}\cdot s_{i} = (\rho(\lambda_{i})\otimes\mathbf{1}_{M})$ in $M^{f}$ where $\rho : K \to B$ is the map giving $B$ its $K$-algebra structure. Hence $x$ is in the span of $S$ in $M^{f}$ as well.
Given that $B$ is simple, any $k$-algebra homomorphism $f : B\to A$ injective; therefore by finite $K$-dimensionality of $A$, $B$ is finite $K$-dimensional as well.
Let $f,g : B \to A$ be two $K$-algebra homomorphisms. Then $M^{f}$ and $M^{g}$ are isomorphic as $B\otimes_{K}\mathrm{End}_{A}M$-module.
nodes.label: lem:iso-fg

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:iso-of-dim-eq}, it is sufficient to prove $\dim_{K}M^{f}=\dim_{K}M^{g}$. But as $K$-vector space, $M^{f}$ and $M^{g}$ are {\em literally\/} $M$.

nodes.name: Skolem-Noether
nodes.statement: Let $f, g : B \to A$ be two $K$-algebra homomorphism. Then $f$ and $g$ differ only by a conjugation. That is there exists a unit $x \in A^{\times}$ such that $g = x f x^{-1}$.
nodes.label: thm:skolem-noether

nodes.statement: Let $M$ be any simple $A$-module (which exists by~\cref{lem:exists-simple-mod}). By~\cref{lem:iso-fg}, we have some isomorphism $\phi : M^{f}\cong M^{g}$ as $B\otimes_{K}\mathrm{End}_{A}M$-module. Since $M$ is simple, we have that $M$ is a balanced $A$-module by~\cref{lem:iso-end-end}. Let $e$ denote the $k$-algerba isomorphism $A \cong \mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$ given by the $A$-action on $M$. Since both $\phi$ and $\phi^{-1}$ defines an element of $\mathrm{End}_{\mathrm{End}_{A}M}M$, we define $a := e^{-1}(\phi)$ and $b := e^{-1}(\phi^{-1})$. Then $ab = 1$ since $e(ab)=e(a)\cdot e(b)=\phi\phi^{-1}=1$. We prove that the image of $f$ and $afb$ under $e$ are the same; that is for all $x\in B$ and $m\in M$, $e(g(x))(m) = e(a f(x) b)(m)$. The right hand side is equal to \[ \begin{aligned} e(af(x)b)(m) &=\left(e(a)\circ e(f(x))\circ e(b)\right)(m) \\ &=\left(\phi\circ e(f(x))\circ \phi^{-1}\right)(m)\\ &=\phi\left(f(x)\cdot\phi^{-1}(m)\right) \\ \end{aligned}. \] Similarly, the left hand side is equal to $g(x)\cdot m$. Note that $\phi$ is $B\otimes \mathrm{End}_{A}M$-linear. Therefore $\phi\left(\left(x\otimes\mathbf{1}\right)\cdot \phi^{-1}(m)\right) = \left(x\otimes\mathbf{1}\right)\cdot m$. Unfolding the definition of $M^{f}$ and $M^{g}$, we see this is saying precisely $\phi\left(f(x)\cdot\phi^{-1}(m)\right)=g(x)\cdot m$.
The centralizer of $\mathcal{L}_{A}$ in $\mathrm{End}_{F}A$ is smaller than or equal to $\mathcal{R}_{A}$: \[ C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}A}\left(\mathcal{L}_{A}\right) \le \mathcal{R}_{A}. \]
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-mul-left-le

nodes.statement: Indeed, let $x \in C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}A}\left(\mathcal{L}_{A}\right)$. Recall from~\cref{con:self-tensor-opp-iso-end} that $e : A\otimes_{F}A^{\mathsf{opp}}\cong \mathrm{End}_{F}A$ as $F$-algebras. Then $e^{-1}(x)$ is in $C_{A\otimes_{F}A^{\mathsf{opp}}}\left(\mathrm{im}\left(A\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\mathsf{opp}}\right)\right)$ (for $e$ sends $a\otimes 1$ to the $F$-linear map $(a\cdot\bullet)$). Since $C_{A\otimes_{F}A^{\mathsf{opp}}}\left(\mathrm{im}\left(A\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\mathsf{opp}}\right)\right) = Z(A)\otimes_{F}A^{\mathsf{opp}}=F\otimes_{F}A^{\mathsf{opp}}=\mathrm{im}\left(A^{\mathsf{opp}}\to A\otimes_{F}A^{\mathsf{opp}}\right)$, we find some $y\in A^{\mathsf{opp}}$ such that $1 \otimes y = e^{-1}(x)$. Therefore $e\left(1\otimes y\right) = x$; but $e\left(1\otimes y\right)$ is in $\mathcal{R}_{A}$ for it is the linear map $(\bullet\cdot y)$.

For any $F$-algebra $B$, every element in $C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}B}\left(\mathcal{L}_{B}\right)$ is in fact $Z(B)$-linear. Let $x\in C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}B}\left(\mathcal{L}_{B}\right)$, $z\in Z(B)$ and $b \in B$, we have $x(z\cdot b) = z\cdot x(b)$ because $x$ commutes with the linear map $\left(z\cdot\bullet\right)$.
nodes.label: rem:mul-left-center-linear

nodes.statement: $A$ is a $Z(A)$-algebra whose algebra structure is given by $Z(A)\hookrightarrow A$. By~\cref{lem:center-simple-ring}, $Z(A)$ is a field. $A$ is finite dimensional as a $Z(A)$-module because of the tower $A/Z(A)/F$.
As $F$-algebras, we have $\mathcal{R}_{A}\cong A^{\mathsf{opp}}$.
nodes.label: lem:mul-right-iso-opp

nodes.statement: We prove the map $A^{\mathsf{opp}} \to \mathcal{R}_{A}$ is bijective. It is injective because if $\left(\bullet \cdot a\right) = \left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$, then $a = 1 \cdot a = 1 \cdot b = b$. The map is surjective by the definition of $\mathcal{R}_{A}$.
Let $B$ be any simple $F$-algebra ({\em not\/} necessarily central). The centralizer of $\mathcal{L}_{B}$ in $\mathrm{End}_{F}B$ is equal to $\mathcal{R}_{B}$.
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-mul-left-eq-mul-right

nodes.statement: It is straightforward to show $\mathcal{R}_{B}^{F}\le C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}A}\left(\mathcal{L}_{B}^{F}\right)$. So we only need to prove $C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}A}\left(\mathcal{L}_{B}^{F}\right)\le \mathcal{R}_{B}^{F}$. By~\cref{lem:centralizer-mul-left-le}, since $B$ is a central simple finite dimensional $Z(B)$-algebra, we have that \[ C_{\mathrm{End}_{Z(B)}B}\left(\mathcal{L}_{B}^{Z(B)}\right) \le \mathcal{R}_{B}^{Z(B)}. \] Suppose $f\in\mathrm{End}_{F}B$ is in $C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}B}B$, by~\cref{rem:mul-left-center-linear}, $f$ is $Z(B)$-linear as well. Then $f$ is in $\mathcal{R}_{B}^{Z(B)}$; that is $f$ is equal to $\left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$ for some $b \in B$ as $Z(B)$-linear maps. Then $f$ is also equal to $\left(\bullet\cdot b\right)$ as $F$-linear maps.
Let $B$ be any $F$-algebra, $x \in B^{\times}$ and $S\subseteq B$ be an $F$-subalgebra of $B$, then $C_{B}(xSx^{-1})=x\left(C_{B}(S)\right)x^{-1}$.
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-conj

nodes.statement: If $a \in C_{B}\left(xSx^{-1}\right)$, then $x^{-1}ax$ is in $C_{B}(S)$. Conversely if $a$ is equal to $xbx^{-1}$ with $b\in C_{B}(S)$, then it is in $C_{B}\left(xSx^{-1}\right)$ as well.

For any finite dimensional $F$-module $B$, we have isomorphism $\mathrm{End}_{F}B \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{\dim_{F}B}F$ as $F$-algebras. Hence $\mathrm{End}_{F} B$ is a finite-dimensional central simple algebra over $F$.
Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra, then $A \otimes_{F} \mathcal{R}_{S}$ is a simple ring.
nodes.label: lem:tensor-mul-right-simple

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:mul-right-iso-opp}, we have $A\otimes \mathcal{R}_{S}\cong A\otimes S^{\mathsf{opp}}$ as $F$-algebras. The claim follows from~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}.

Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra, then there exists an $x\in \left(A\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S\right)^{\times}$ such that $C_{A}(S)\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S$ is isomorphic to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ as $F$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-tensor-end-eq-conj-tensor-mul-right

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:tensor-central} and~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $A \otimes_{F}C_{A}(S)$ is a central simple $F$-algebra. Let $f : S \to A\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S$ be an $F$-algebra homomorphism defined by $s \mapsto s \otimes \mathbf{1}_{S}$ and $g : S \to A \otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S$ be an $F$-algebra homomorphism defined by $\mathbf{1}_{A} \otimes \left(s\cdot\bullet\right)$. Then by~\cref{thm:skolem-noether}, we that there exists some $x\in \left(A\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S\right)^{\times}$ such that $f = xgx^{-1}$. Then we have $S\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S$ is equal to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{L}_{S}\right)x^{-1}$: indeed the left hand side is $\mathrm{im} f$ while the right handside is $x\left(\mathrm{im} g\right)x^{-1}$. Therefore $C_{A\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S}\left(S\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S\right) = C_{A\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S}\left(x\left(A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}\right)x^{-1}\right)$. By~\cref{lem:centralizer-conj}, the right hand side is equal to $xC_{A\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S}\left(A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{L}_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ which is $x\left(A\otimes_{F}C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}S}\left(\mathcal{L}_{S}\right)\right)x^{-1}$ by~\cref{lem:centralizer-inclusion-tensor} which is $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ by~\cref{lem:centralizer-mul-left-eq-mul-right}.
Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra, then $C_{A}(S)$ is simple as well.
nodes.label: lem:simple-centralizer

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-tensor-end-eq-conj-tensor-mul-right}, $C_{A}(S) \otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S$ is isomorphic to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ as $F$-algebras. Then $C(S)\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S$ is simple since $A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}$ is simple by~\cref{lem:tensor-mul-right-simple}. By~\cref{thm:tensor-simple-implies-simple}, $C_{A}(S)$ is simple.
Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra. Then \[ \dim_{F}C_{A}(S)\cdot\dim_{F}S=\dim_{F}A. \]
nodes.label: lem:dim-centralizer

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:centralizer-tensor-end-eq-conj-tensor-mul-right}, $C_{A}(S) \otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S$ is isomorphic to $x\left(A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}\right)x^{-1}$ as $F$-algebras. Hence $\dim_{F}\left(C_{A}(S)\otimes_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S\right)=\dim_{F}\left(A\otimes_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}\right)$ where the left hand side is $\dim_{F}C_{A}(S)\cdot \dim_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S$ and the right hand side is $\dim_{F}A\cdot\dim_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}$. Since $\dim_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}S=\dim_{F}S^{2}$ and $\dim_{F}\mathcal{R}_{S}=\dim S$ (by~\cref{lem:mul-right-iso-opp}), we proved this lemma.
Let $S \subseteq A$ be a central simple $F$-subalgebra, \[ A \cong B \otimes_{F} C_{A}(B). \]
nodes.label: cor:self-tensor-centralizer

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, $C_{A}(B)$ is simple and by~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $B \otimes_{F} C_{A}(B)$ is simple. Hence the map $B \otimes_{F} C_{A}(B) \to A$ induced by $B \hookrightarrow A$ and $C_{A}(B) \hookrightarrow A$ is injective. By~\cref{cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq}, we only need to show $\dim_{F}B\otimes_{F}C_{A}(B) =\dim_{F}A$ which is precisely~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}.

nodes.name: Double Centralizer
nodes.statement: Let $S\subseteq A$ be a simple $F$-subalgebra, we have \[ C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right) = S. \]
nodes.label: thm:double-centralizer

nodes.statement: It is straightforward that $S \le C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right)$. By~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, $C_{A}(S)$ is simple, hence $\dim_{F}C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right)\cdot \dim_{F}C_{A}(S)=\dim_{F}A=\dim_{F}C_{A}(S)\cdot \dim_{F}S$ (by applying~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer} twice), i.e. $\dim_{F}C_{A}\left(C_{A}(S)\right) = \dim_{F}S$. This equality of dimension gives us the desired result.

By~\cref{lem:tensor-central} and~\cref{thm:tensor-csa}, $\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}$ is closed under tensor product, that is if $A, B\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}$, we have $A\otimes_{K} B\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}$ as well.

nodes.name: Brauer Equivalence
nodes.statement: For any two $A, B\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}$, we say $A$ and $B$ are Brauer equivalent, when there exists $m, n \in \mathbb{N}_{\ge0}$ such that $\mathrm{Mat}_{m}(A)\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}B$ as $K$-algebras. We denote this relation as $A\sim_{\mathrm{Br}_{K}} B$, when $K$ is clear, we drop the subscript.
nodes.label: def:br-eqv

nodes.statement: Isomorphic $K$-algebras are Brauer equivalent.
$\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}$ is reflexive.
Indeed, $A \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{1}(A)$ as $K$-algerbas.
$\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}$ is symmetric.
Indeed, just exchange $m$ and $n$.
$\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}$ is transitive.

Let $A\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}B$ and $B\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}C$; that is for some $m,n,p, q\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge0}$ we have $\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(A)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{m}(B)$ and $\mathrm{Mat}_{p}(B)\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{q}(C)$ as $K$-algebras. Hence, from~\cref{con:matrix-matrix}, we have the following: \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Mat}_{np}(A)&\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{p}\left(\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(A)\right)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{p}\left(\mathrm{Mat}_{m}(B)\right)\\ &\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{mp}(B)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{m}\left(\mathrm{Mat}_{p}(B)\right)\\ &\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{m}\left(\mathrm{Mat}_{q}(C)\right)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{mq}(C). \end{aligned} \] In another word, $A\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}C$.
$(\bullet\otimes_{K}\bullet):\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}\times\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A} \to \mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}$ descends to a function on $\mathrm{Br}(K)$.
nodes.label: lem:br-mul-wd

nodes.statement: We need to prove that for all $A, B, C, D \in \mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}$ such that $A\sim_{\mathrm{Br}} B$ and $C\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}D$, $A\otimes_{R}C \sim_{\mathrm{Br}} B\otimes_{R}D$ as well. Suppose $\mathrm{Mat}_{m}(A)\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(B)$ as $K$-algebras and $\mathrm{Mat}_{p}(C)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{q}(D)$, by~\cref{con:matrix-tensor-matrix}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{Mat}_{mp}\left(A\otimes_{R} C\right)&\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{m}(A)\otimes_{R}\mathrm{Mat}_{p}(C) \\ &\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(B)\otimes_{R}\mathrm{Mat}_{q}(D)\\ &\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{nq}\left(B\otimes_{R}D\right). \end{aligned} \]
If $K$ is algebraically closed, $\mathrm{Br}(K)$ is trivial; in particular $\mathrm{Br}_{n}(\mathbb{C})$ is trivial.
nodes.label: thm:br-triv-alg-closed

nodes.statement: We need to show that every $A\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(K)$ for some $K$ when $K$ is algebraically closed. Indeed, by~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, $A \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$ for some division algebra $D$ and $n\in\mathbb{N}_{\ge0}$. Since $K$ is algebraically closed and $D$ is an integral domain and finite dimensional, the structure morphism $\rho: K\to D$ is a isomorphism; therefore $A\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(K)$.

Let $A, B \in \mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{K}$. There exists a division $K$-algebra $D$ and non-zero $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{m}(D)$ and $B\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$ as $K$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:common-div-alg

nodes.statement: By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, we can find division algebras $S_{A}, S_{B}$ and non-zero $m, n\in\mathbb{N}$ such that $A\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{n}\left(S_{A}\right)$ and $B\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{m}\left(S_{B}\right)$ as $K$-algebras. Hence $B\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}A\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}\mathrm{Mat}_{n}\left(S_{A}\right)\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}S_{A}$, in another word, for some non-zero $a, a'\in\mathbb{N}$, we have $\mathrm{Mat}_{a}(B)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{a'}\left(S_{A}\right)$ as $K$-algebras. Hence, by~\cref{thm:wed-artin-uniq}, we have that $S_{A}\cong S_{B}$ as $K$-algebras and the lemma is proved.
$\mathrm{Br}_{K}^{K}$ is identity.
nodes.label: lem:br-base-change-self

nodes.statement: If $A\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}$, then $A\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}K\otimes_{K}A$.
Consider the tower of field extension $E/F/K$, \[ \mathrm{Br}_{K}^{E} = \mathrm{Br}_{E}^{F}\circ\mathrm{Br}_{K}^{E}. \]
nodes.label: lem:br-base-change-tower

nodes.statement: If $A\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{K}$, then $E\otimes_{F}\left(F\otimes_{K}A\right)$ is isomorphic to $E \otimes_{F} A$ as $E$-algebras.
$\mathrm{Br}$ forms a functor from category of field to category of abelian groups.
This is the categorical version of~\cref{lem:br-base-change-self} and~\cref{lem:br-base-change-tower}.

nodes.name: Relative Brauer Group
nodes.statement: Let $E/K$ be a field extension, we define the relative Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(E/K)$ to be the kernel of the base change morphism $\mathrm{Br}_{K}^{E}$.

Unpacking the definition of the relative Brauer group, we see that for any $A \in \mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{K}$, if $E\otimes_{K}A\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(E)$ as $E$-algebras, then $\mathrm{Br}^{E}_{K}\left([A]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}\right)=1$.

nodes.name: Splitting Field
nodes.statement: For any field extension $E/K$ and any $K$-algebra $A$, we say $E$ is a splitting field of $A$ if and only if $E\otimes_{K}A \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(E)$ as $E$-algebras for some non-zero $n$. We also say $E$ splits $A$ or $A$ is splited by $E$
Let $E/K$ be a field extension and $A\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{K}$, $E$ splits $A$ if and only if $[A]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}\in\mathrm{Br}(E/K)$.
nodes.label: thm:split-iff-mem-relative

nodes.statement: The ``only if'' part is by definition. For the other direction, we know by definition that $\mathrm{Mat}_{n}(E\otimes_{K}A)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{m}(E)$ as $E$-algebras for some non-zero $m, n$. By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-algebra}, we find some division algebra $D$ and non-zero natural number $p$ such that $E\otimes_{K}A\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{p}(D)$ as $E$-algebras. Thus $\mathrm{Mat}_{pm}(E)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{pn}\left(E\otimes_{K}A\right)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{p^{2}n}(D)$ as $E$-algebras. By~\cref{thm:wed-artin-uniq}, we conclude that $E\cong D$ as $E$-algebras. Hence $E\otimes_{K}A\cong \mathrm{Mat}_{p}(E)$, in another word, $E$ splits $A$.

In light of~\cref{lem:br-base-change-tower}, if $K$ is algebraic closed then $K$ splits any $K$-algebra $A$. Indeed, $K$ splits $A$ if and only if $[A]_{\sim\mathrm{Br}}$ but $[A]_{\sim\mathrm{Br}}$ is equal to $1$.

If two $\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{K}$ are Brauer equivalent, in another word, $A \sim_{\mathrm{Br}_{K}} B$, then $E$ splits $A$ if and only if $E$ splits $B$. Indeed, if $A$ and $B$ are equivalent, then $[A]_{\sim\mathrm{Br}} \in \mathrm{Br}(E/K)$ if and only if $[B]_{\sim\mathrm{Br}}\in\mathrm{Br}(E/K)$.

Let $A\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{F}$ splitted by $K$. There exists a $B\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{F}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $[A]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}[B]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}=1$ \item there exists $F$-algebra map $K\hookrightarrow B$ \item ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F}B$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: lem:good-rep-inv

nodes.statement: Since $K$ splits $A$, we find a non-zero natural number $n$ such that $K\otimes_{F}A\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{n}K\cong\mathrm{End}_{K}\left(K^{n}\right)$ as $K$-algebras. We define an $F$-algebra map $\iota: A\to\mathrm{End}_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)$ by \begin{center} \begin{tikzcd} A \arrow{r} & K \otimes_{F} A \arrow{r}{\cong} & \mathrm{End}_K\left(K^n\right) \arrow{r}{|_{F}} & \mathrm{End}_F\left(K^n\right) \end{tikzcd}, \end{center} where $|_{F}$ is restriction of scalars. Since $A$ is simple, $\iota$ is injective, therefore $A \cong \iota(A)$ as $F$-algebras. Define $B$ as $C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}(\iota(A))$, the centralizer of the range of $\iota$ in $\mathrm{End}_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)$. We construct an embedding $K \hookrightarrow B$ by $r \mapsto (r \cdot \bullet)$ $B$ is a central $F$-algebra: if $x \in Z(B)$, then $x \in \iota(A)$ because by~\cref{thm:double-centralizer}, it is sufficient to prove that $x$ is in $C_{\mathrm{End}_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}\left(B\right)$ which follows from the fact that $x \in Z(B)$. In fact, $x \in Z(\iota(A))$: suppose $a \in A$, we need to check $x \cdot \iota(a) = \iota(a)\cdot x$, this is the case because $B$ is defined as the centralizer of $\iota(A)$. Since $\iota(A) \cong A$ as $F$-algebras, $\iota(A)$ is $F$-central, hence $x \in F$. $B$ is a simple ring: by~\cref{lem:simple-centralizer}, it is sufficient to prove that $\iota(A)$ is a simple ring which comes from $A \cong \iota(A)$ as $F$-algebras. By~\cref{cor:self-tensor-centralizer}, we have $F$-algebra isomorphism $\mathrm{End}_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\cong \iota(A)\otimes_{F}B \cong A \otimes_{F}B$. Since $\mathrm{End}_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{\dim_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)}\left(F\right)$ as $F$-algebras, we see that $[A]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}$ and $[B]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}$ are inverses. By~\cref{lem:dim-centralizer}, $\dim_{F}B\cdot \dim_{F}\iota(A) = \dim_{F}B\cdot\dim_{F}A = \dim_{F}\mathrm{End}_{F}\left(K^{n}\right) = {\left(\dim_{F}\left(K^{n}\right)\right)}^{2}={\left(\dim_{F}K\cdot \dim_{K}\left(K^{n}\right)\right)}^{2}=n^{2}\cdot{\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. On the other hand, since $K\otimes_{F}A\cong\mathrm{Mat}_{n}K$, we have $\dim_{F}K\otimes_{F}A=\dim_{F}K\cdot\dim_{F}A=\dim_{F}\mathrm{Mat}_{n}K=\dim_{F}K\dim_{K}\mathrm{Mat}_{n}K=n^{2}\dim_{F}K$. Since $\dim_{F}K\ne 0$ , we conclude $\dim_{F}A=n^{2}$. Since $n\ne 0$ and $\dim_{F}(B)\cdot \dim_{F}(A)=n^{2}\dim_{F}(B)=n^{2}{\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$, we get the desired result.

Let $A\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{F}$ splitted by $K$. There exists a $B \in \mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{F}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $[B]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}=[A]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}$ \item there exists an $F$-algebra map $K\hookrightarrow B$ \item ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F}B$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: cor:good-rep

nodes.statement: Let $B$ and $\iota : K \hookrightarrow B$ be as in~\cref{lem:good-rep-inv}. Consider $B^{\mathsf{opp}}$ and $K \hookrightarrow B \to B^{\mathsf{opp}}$. This works.

Let $A\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{F}$. $K$ splits $A$ if and only if there exists a $B\in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{F}$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $[B]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}=[A]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}$ \item there exists an $F$-algebra map $K \hookrightarrow B$ \item ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F}B$. \end{itemize}
nodes.label: thm:good-rep-iff-split

nodes.statement: The ``if'' direction is~\cref{cor:good-rep}. For the ``only if'' direction, let $B \in\mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{F}$ and $\iota : K \hookrightarrow B$ be given. We give $B$ a $K$-module structure by right multiplication, that is for any $a \in K$ and $b \in B$, we define $a \cdot b := b \cdot \iota(a)$. Since $B$ is a finite dimensional $F$-vector space and $K/F$ is a finite dimensional field extension, $B$ is a finite dimensional $K$-vector space as well. Since $[B]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}=[A]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}}$, it is sufficient to show that $K$ splits $B$. We define an $F$-bilinear map $\mu : K \to B \to \mathrm{End}_{K}B$ by $(c, a) \mapsto (c \cdot a \cdot \bullet)$ which induce an $F$-linear map $\mu' : K \otimes_{F} B \to \mathrm{End}_{K}B$. Since for any $r, c\in K$ and $a \in B$, we have $\mu'\left(r \cdot c\otimes a\right)(a') = a a' \iota(rc)=aa'\iota(c)\iota(r)=r\cdot \mu'(c\otimes a)$, that is $\mu'$ is $K$-linear as well. Note that \[\mu'(1)=\mu'(1\otimes 1) = (1\cdot 1\cdot \bullet) = 1\] and that \[ \begin{aligned} \mu'(c\otimes a \cdot c'\otimes a')(a'') &= \mu'(cc'\otimes aa')(a'') \\ &= cc' \cdot aa' \cdot a'' \\ &= aa' a'' \iota(c c') \\ &= a(a' a'' \iota(c'))\iota(c) \\ &=\mu'(c \otimes a)(a' a'' \iota(c'))\\ &=\mu'(c\otimes a)\left(\mu'(c'\otimes a')(a'')\right) \\ &= \left(\mu'(c\otimes a)\circ\mu'(c'\otimes a')\right)(a'') \end{aligned}, \] that is, $\mu'$ is an $K$-algebra map. If we can show that $\mu'$ is a bijection, we will prove the result for $K\otimes_{F} B \cong \mathrm{End}_{K} B \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{\dim_{K} B}K$ as $K$-algebras. By~\cref{cor:alghom-bijective-of-dim-eq}, it is sufficient to show $\dim_{K}K\otimes_{F}B = \dim_{K}\mathrm{End}_{K}B$. Let $n$ denote $\dim_{F}K$. Since, $\dim_{F}K\dim_{K}K\otimes_{F}B =\dim_{F}K\otimes_{F}B=\dim_{F}K \dim_{F}B$. we have $\dim_{K}K\otimes_{F}B = \dim_{F}B = {\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. On the other hand, since ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}=\dim_{F} B = \dim_{F}K\dim_{K}B$, we have $\dim_{K} B = \dim_{F}K$; thus $\dim_{K}\mathrm{End}_{K} B = {\left(\dim_{K}B\right)}^{2}={\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$ and the result is proved.

nodes.name: Good Representation
nodes.statement: For any $X \in \mathrm{Br}(F)$, a $K$-good representation of $X$ is an $A \in \mathsf{C}\!\mathsf{S}\!\mathsf{A}_{F}$ and an $F$-algebra map $K \hookrightarrow A$ such that $[A]_{\sim_{\mathrm{Br}}} = X$ and $\dim_{F}A={\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$. We often denote the $F$-algebra map $K \hookrightarrow A$ as $\iota$ or $\iota_{A}$.
nodes.label: def:good-rep

nodes.statement: For any $X\in\mathrm{Br}(F)$, $X\in\mathrm{Br}(K/F)$ if and only if $X$ admits a good representation.
nodes.label: cor:mem-relative-br-iff-good-rep

nodes.statement: Rephrase of~\cref{thm:good-rep-iff-split} and~\cref{thm:split-iff-mem-relative}.
The range $\iota_{A}(A)$ is a simple ring.
Because $K$ is a simple ring, $\iota_{A}$ is injective therefore $\iota_{A}(A)\cong K$.
$C_{A}\left(\iota_{A}(A)\right) = \iota_{A}(A)$.
nodes.label: lem:centralizer-range-good-rep

nodes.statement: In the language of~\cref{sec:subfield}, $\iota_{A}(A)$ is a subfield of $A$, hence by~\cref{lem:tfae-subfield}, we only need to show $\dim_{F}A = {\left(\dim_{F}\iota_{A}(A)\right)}^{2}$. But $\dim_{F}A={\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$ and $\iota(A)\cong K$.
If $A$ and $B$ are two good representations of $X$, then $A \cong B$ as $F$-algebras.
nodes.label: lem:good-rep-iso

nodes.statement: By~\cref{lem:common-div-alg}, we find a division $F$-algebra $D$ and non-zero natural numbers $m, n$ such that $A \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{m}(D)$ and $B \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{n}(D)$ as $F$-algebras. Therefore \[ \begin{aligned} {\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2} &= \dim_{F}A &= m^{2}\dim_{F}D \\ &= \dim_{F}B &= n^{2}\dim_{F}D. \end{aligned} \] Therefore $m = n$ and $A \cong \mathrm{Mat}_{m}D =\mathrm{Mat}_{n}D\cong B$.
Since $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ acts on $K^{\star}$, for $x\in K^{\star}$,we feel free to write $\sigma\cdot x$ when it feels more readable than $\sigma(x)$, for example when there are nested brackets.

nodes.name: Conjugation Factor
nodes.statement: With respect to $A$, a conjugation factor of $\sigma$ is a unit $x_{\sigma} \in A^{\star}$ such that for all $c \in K$, \[ x_{\sigma} \iota_{A}(c)x_{\sigma}^{-1} = \iota_{A}(\sigma \cdot c). \] A conjugation sequence is a sequence $x:\mathrm{Gal}(K/F) \to A^{\star}$ such that for all $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, $x_{\sigma}$ is a conjugation factor of $\sigma$. When we want to stress $A$, we say $A$-conjugation factor and $A$-conjugation sequence.
nodes.label: def:conj-factor

nodes.statement: When $x_{\sigma}$ is a conjugation factor of $\sigma$, the equalities $x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}(c) = x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}(\sigma(c))$ and $\iota_{A}(c)x_{\sigma}^{-1}=x_{\sigma}^{-1}\iota_{A}(\sigma(c))$ are also useful.
nodes.label: rem:conj-factor-alternative-eq

nodes.statement: If $x$ is an $A$-conjugation sequence, then $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ is an $K$-linearly independent set. When $K/F$ is finite dimensional and Galois, $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ is a $K$-basis for $A$.
nodes.label: thm:conj-seq-basis

nodes.statement: Suppose $\{x_{\sigma}\}$ is linearly dependent. Let $J \subseteq \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ be such that $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in J\}$ is a maximally linearly independent subset. Then $J \ne \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, let $\sigma \in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ be an arbitrary automorphism that is not in $J$. Since $\{x_{\tau}|\tau\in J\}$ is maximally linearly independent, $x_\sigma \in \left\langle x_{\tau}|\tau\in J\right\rangle$. Hence, by~\cref{con:good-rep-mod} we have \[ x_\sigma = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau} = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)x_{\tau}, \] for some non-zero $\lambda_{\tau}\in K$ and $J' \subseteq J$. For each $c \in K$, we have the following equality \[ \begin{aligned} \iota_{A}\left(\sigma \cdot c\right) x_{\sigma} &= x_{\sigma} \iota_{A}(c) &\text{by~\cref{def:conj-factor}}\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau}\iota_{A}(c) & \\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot \iota_{A}\left(\tau\cdot c\right)x_{\tau} &\text{by~\cref{def:conj-factor} again}\\ &=\sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c)\right)x_{\tau};\\ \iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot c\right)x_{\sigma} &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right) x_{\tau}\iota_{A}(c)\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J'}\iota_{A}\left(\sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau}\right)x_{\tau}. \end{aligned} \] Since $\{x_{\tau}|\tau\in J'\}$ is linearly independent, we have that for each $\tau \in J'$, $\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c) = \sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau} = \lambda_{\tau}\sigma(c)$. Note that $J'$ is not empty, for otherwise $x_{\sigma}=\sum_{\tau\in\emptyset}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot x_{\tau}=0$ but $x_{\sigma}$ is invertible. Since for any $\tau\in J'$, $\lambda_{\tau}$ is not zero, we have that for all $c \in K$, $\sigma(c) = \tau(c)$, i.e. $\sigma = \tau$. Hence $\sigma$ is in $J' \subseteq J$ after all; contradiction. If $K/F$ is finite dimensional and Galois, then $\dim_{F}K$ is equal to the cardinality of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, then by the linear independence of $\{x_{\sigma}|\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$, we conclude that it is indeed a $K$-basis for $A$.

nodes.name: the Second Group Cohomology
nodes.statement: Let $G$ be a group and $M$ an abelian group (written multiplicatively) with a $G$-action. A function $f : G \times G \to M$ is a {\em 2-cocycle\/} if for all $g,h,j\in G$, \[ f(gh, j)f(g, h) = \left(g\cdot f(h, j)\right) f(g, hj). \] We denote the subgroup of 2-cocycles as $\mathcal{Z}^{2}(G, M)$. A function $f : G\times G \to M$ is a {\em 2-coboundary\/} if there exists an $x : G \to M$ such that for all $g, h \in G$ \[ \frac{g\cdot x(h)}{x(gh)} x(g) = f(g, h). \] We denote the subgroup of 2-coboundaries as $\mathcal{B}^{2}(G, M)$. The second group cohomology $\mathrm{H}^{2}\left(G, M\right)$ is defined to be the quotient group of 2-cocycles modulo 2-coboundaries $^{\mathcal{Z}^{2}(G, M)}/_{\mathcal{B}^{2}(G, M)}$. If $s, t \in \mathcal{Z}^{2}(G, M)$, we say $s$ and $t$ are cohomologous if their equivalence class $[s], [t] \in \mathrm{H}^{2}(G, M)$ are the same; in another word $st^{-1}\in\mathcal{B}^{2}(G, M)$.
nodes.label: def:second-group-coh

nodes.statement: If $f \in \mathcal{B}^{2}(G, M)$ is a 2-cocycle and $x\in G$, we have \[ \begin{aligned} f(1, x) &= f(1, 1) \\ f(x, 1) &= x\cdot f(1, 1). \end{aligned} \]
nodes.label: lem:2-cocycle-one-one

nodes.statement: Indeed: \[ \begin{aligned} f(1\cdot 1, x)f(1, 1) &= (1\cdot f(1,x))f(1, 1\cdot x) \\ f(1, x)f(1, 1) &= f(1, x) f(1,x) \\ f(1, x) &= f(1,1) \end{aligned} \] and \[ \begin{aligned} f(x\cdot 1, 1)f(x, 1) &= (x\cdot f(1, 1))f(x, 1\cdot 1)\\ f(x, 1)f(x, 1) &= (x\cdot f(1, 1))f(x, 1)\\ f(x, 1) &= x \cdot f(1, 1). \end{aligned} \]

nodes.name: Twisting Conjugation Factors
nodes.statement: If $x$ and $y$ are two conjugation factors of $\sigma$, then there exists a unique $c \in K$ such that $x = y\iota_{A}(c)$.
nodes.label: lem:twist-spec1

nodes.statement: The uniqueness is clear: suppose $x = y\iota_{A}(c)=y\iota_{A}(c')$, then $c = c'$ because $x, y$ are units and $\iota_{A}$ is injective. We first observe that $y^{-1}x\in C_{A}(\iota(A))$: for any $z \in K$, $y^{-1}x\iota_{A}(z)=y^{-1}\iota_{A}(\sigma(z))x=\iota_{A}(z)y^{-1}x$ (by~\cref{rem:conj-factor-alternative-eq}). By~\cref{lem:centralizer-range-good-rep}, $y^{-1}x\in \iota(A)$, that is for some $z \in K$, we have that $y^{-1}x = \iota_{A}(z)$ and the claim is proved.
$\mathrm{twist}(x, x)$ is equal to $1$ by uniqueness.
In fact, $\mathrm{twist}(x, y)$ is in $K^{\star}$ and $\mathrm{twist}(x, y)^{-1}=\mathrm{twist}(y, x)$.
If $x$ and $y$ are conjugation factors for $\sigma$, $x=\iota_{A}(\sigma(\mathrm{twist}_{x, y}))y$.
nodes.label: lem:twist-spec2

nodes.statement: \[ \begin{aligned} x &= x \iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{twist}_{x,y}\right) x^{-1} x \iota_{A}(\mathrm{twist}_{y,x}) \\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot\mathrm{twist}_{x,y}\right)x\iota_{A}\left( \mathrm{twist}_{y,x}\right)\\ &=\iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot \mathrm{twist}_{x,y}\right)y \end{aligned}. \]

Let $x : \mathrm{Gal}(K/F) \to A^{\star}$ be a conjugation sequence. We have \[ \mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho}, x_{\sigma}, x_{\rho\sigma}}\,\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}} = \rho\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho}, x_{\sigma\tau}, x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}. \]
nodes.label: lem:compare-conj-factor-spec

nodes.statement: It is sufficient to make the following calculations: \begin{align} x_{\rho}\,x_{\sigma}x_{\tau} &= \iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma},x_{\rho\sigma}}\right) \, \iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho\sigma}, x_{\tau}, x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)\, x_{\rho\sigma\tau}\\ x_{\rho}\left(x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}\right) &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right) x_{\rho\sigma\tau} \end{align} Then since $x_{\rho\sigma\tau}$ is invertible and $\iota_{A}$ is injective, we proved the desired result. \Cref{eq:1} is because: by the first equality in~\cref{con:compare-conj-factors} (twice) \[ x_{\rho}x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}=\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma}, x_{\rho\sigma}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma}x_{\tau}=\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma},x_{\rho\sigma}}\right)\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma\tau}. \] \Cref{eq:2} is because: by~\cref{def:conj-factor}, we have \[\iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho}=x_{\rho}\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right),\] therefore by~\cref{con:br-base-change} \[ \begin{aligned} x_{\rho}\left(x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}\right) &= x_{\rho}\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau} \\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot \mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho}x_{\sigma\tau}\\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\rho\cdot\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\,\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\rho},x_{\sigma\tau},x_{\rho\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\rho\sigma\tau} \end{aligned}. \]
For any $A$-conjugation sequence $x$, $\mathcal{B}^{2}_{x} \in \mathcal{B}^{2}\left(\mathrm{Gal}(K/F), K^{\star}\right)$, that is $\mathcal{B}_{x}$ is indeed a 2-cocycle.

We need to prove \[ \mathcal{B}_{x}(\rho\sigma, \tau)\, \mathcal{B}_{x}(\rho,\sigma) = \rho\left(\mathcal{B}_{x}(\sigma, \tau)\right)\, \mathcal{B}_{x}(\rho, \sigma\tau). \] But this is exactly~\cref{lem:compare-conj-factor-spec}.
For any $c \in K$, $\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ and $A$-conjugation factor $x$ of $\sigma$, we have \[ \iota_{B}\left(\sigma\cdot c\right) = ue(x)u^{-1}\,\iota_{B}(c)\,ue\left(x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}. \]
nodes.label: lem:iso-conj-coeff-spec2

nodes.statement: From~\cref{def:conj-factor}, we have $e\left(\iota_{A}(\sigma \cdot c)\right) = e\left(x\iota_{A}(c)x^{-1}\right)$. Substituting it in~\cref{con:good-rep-iso-coeff}, we get \[ \begin{aligned} \iota_{B}(\sigma \cdot c) &= ue\left(x\iota_{A}(c)x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}\\ &= ue(x)e\left(\iota_{A}(c)\right)e\left(x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}\\ &= ue(x)u^{-1}\iota_{B}(c)ue\left(x^{-1}\right)u^{-1}. \end{aligned} \]

Let $x$ be an $A$-conjugation sequence and $y$ a $B$-conjugation sequence. We have \[ \mathrm{comp}_{y_{\sigma}, y_{\tau}, y_{\sigma\tau}} v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}} = v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}} \sigma\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right) \mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}. \]
nodes.label: lem:compare-to-2-cocycle-aux

nodes.statement: By~\cref{con:compare-conj-factors}, we have $y_{\sigma}y_{\tau} = \iota_{B}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)y_{\sigma\tau}$. By repeated application of~\cref{con:push-forward-conj-factor} and~\cref{con:good-rep-iso-coeff}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} y_{\sigma\tau}&= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ y_{\sigma}y_{\tau} &= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\right)x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)x_{\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= \iota_{B}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)y_{\sigma\tau}\\ &= \iota_{B}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= u\,e\left(\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)\right)\,u^{-1}\,\,\,ue\left(\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)\,u^{-1}\\ &= ue\left(\iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\right)u^{-1}. \end{aligned} \] Hence \[ \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\right)x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)x_{\tau} = \iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}. \] We also have by~\cref{def:conj-factor} \[ x_{\sigma} \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right) x_{\tau} = \iota_{A}\left(\sigma\cdot v_{x_{\tau}y_{\tau}}\right) x_{\sigma}x_{\tau}. \] Hence \[ \begin{aligned} \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\right)x_{\sigma}\iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)x_{\tau} &= \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\, \sigma\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)\right) x_{\sigma}x_{\tau} \\ &= \iota_{A}\left(v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}}\sigma\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right)\mathrm{comp}_{x_{\sigma},x_{\tau},x_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}\\ &= \iota_{A}\left(\mathrm{comp}_{y_{\sigma},y_{\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}}\right)x_{\sigma\tau}. \end{aligned} \] Cancelling $x_{\sigma\tau}$ and by injectivity of $\iota_{A}$, the result is proved.

Let $x$ be an $A$-conjugation sequence and $y$ a $B$-conjugation sequence. We have \[ \mathcal{B}^{2}_{B,y}(\sigma,\tau) v_{x_{\sigma\tau},y_{\sigma\tau}} = v_{x_{\sigma},y_{\sigma}} \sigma\left(v_{x_{\tau},y_{\tau}}\right) \mathcal{B}^{2}_{A,y}(\sigma,\tau). \]
nodes.label: lem:compare-to-2-cocycle

nodes.statement: If we unfold~\cref{con:good-rep-to-2-cocycles}, we discover the lemma is saying exactly~\cref{lem:compare-to-2-cocycle-aux}.
Let $x$ be an $A$-conjugation sequence and $y$ a $B$-conjugation sequence. $\mathcal{B}^{2}_{A,x}$ and $\mathcal{B}^{2}_{B,y}$ are 2-cohomologous.
nodes.label: cor:to-2-cocycle-wd

nodes.statement: By~\cref{def:second-group-coh}, we need to find a function $f : \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\to K^{\star}$ such that for all $\sigma, \tau\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, \[ \frac{\sigma\left(f(\tau)\right)}{f\left(\sigma\tau\right)}f(\sigma)=\frac{\mathcal{B}^{2}_{B,y}}{\mathcal{B}^{2}_{A,x}}. \] Let $f(\rho) := v_{x_{\rho},y_{\rho}}$, by~\cref{lem:compare-to-2-cocycle} we see the equality holds.

When $K/F$ is infinite dimensional, the correct definition of $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ is perhaps $\bigoplus_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}K$. But in Lean4, function type is easier to manipulate than direct sums. Since our scope is finite dimensional Galois extension, our definition is still accurate.

The cross product $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ is a ring with the multiplicative unit $\Delta_{\mathsf{id}, \mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id}, \mathsf{id})^{-1}}$. The $F$-action on $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ defined by $r \cdot \Delta_{\sigma, c} := \Delta_{\sigma, r\cdot c}$ makes it an $F$-algebra.

We verify the axioms of rings on elements of the form $\Delta_{\sigma, c}$. Let $\sigma,\tau,\rho\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ and $a,b,c\in K$. \begin{itemize} \item associativity of multiplication. We need to check that $\Delta_{\sigma,a}\left(\Delta_{\tau,b}\Delta_{\rho,c}\right) = \left(\Delta_{\sigma,a}\Delta_{\tau,b}\right)\Delta_{\rho,c}$: \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta_{\sigma, a}\left(\Delta_{\tau,b}\Delta_{\rho,c}\right) &= \Delta_{\sigma,a}\Delta_{\tau\rho,b\tau(c) \mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau)}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma\tau\rho,a\sigma(b)\sigma(\tau(c)) \sigma(\mathfrak{a}(\sigma, \tau))};\\ \left(\Delta_{\sigma,a}\Delta_{\tau,b}\right)\Delta_{\rho,c} &= \Delta_{\sigma\tau,a\sigma(b)\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau)}\Delta_{\rho,c}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma\tau\rho,a\sigma(b)\mathfrak{a}(\sigma, \tau)\sigma(\tau(c))\mathfrak{a}(\sigma\tau, \rho)}. \end{aligned} \] Hence it is sufficient to check \[ \sigma(\tau(c))\sigma(\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau)) = \mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau)\sigma(\tau(c))\mathfrak{a}(\sigma\tau, \rho). \] This is the 2-cocycle condition in~\cref{def:second-group-coh} (modulo commutativity of $K$). \item multiplicative unit: we need to check $\Delta_{\sigma, a}\Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id}, \mathsf{id})} = \Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})}\Delta_{\sigma, a} = \Delta_{\sigma, a}$. By multiple applications of~\cref{lem:2-cocycle-one-one} \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id}, \mathsf{id})^{-1}}\Delta_{\sigma, a} &= \Delta_{\sigma, \mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id}, \mathsf{id})^{-1}a\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\sigma)}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma, \mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id}, \mathsf{id}) a\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma, a} \\ \Delta_{\sigma, a}\Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}} &= \Delta_{\sigma, a\sigma(\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id}))^{-1}\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\mathsf{id})}\\ &=\Delta_{\sigma, a\sigma(\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id}))^{-1}\sigma(\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id}, id))}\\ &=\Delta_{\sigma, a} \end{aligned} \] \item distributivity: We need to check left-distributivity $\Delta_{\sigma, a}\left(\Delta_{\tau, b} + \Delta_{\rho, c}\right) = \Delta_{\sigma,a}\Delta_{\tau,b} + \Delta_{\sigma, a}\Delta_{\rho, c}$ and right distributivity $\left(\Delta_{\tau,b} + \Delta_{\rho,c}\right)\Delta_{\sigma,a} = \Delta_{\tau,b}\Delta_{\sigma,a} + \Delta_{\rho,c}\Delta_{\sigma,a}$. This is precisely what ``extend linearly'' means. \item $F$-algebra: We need to check for all $r \in F$, $\left(r\cdot \Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}\right)\Delta_{\sigma,c} = \Delta_{\sigma,c}\left(r\cdot\Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}\right)$. By~\cref{lem:2-cocycle-one-one} \[ \begin{aligned} \left(r\cdot \Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}\right)\Delta_{\sigma,c} &= \Delta_{\mathsf{id},r\cdot\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}\Delta_{\sigma,c}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma,\left(r\cdot\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}\right)c\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\sigma)} \\ &=\Delta_{\sigma,\left(r\cdot\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}\right)c\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})} \\ &= \Delta_{\sigma, r\cdot c}\\ \Delta_{\sigma,c}\left(r\cdot\Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}\right) &= \Delta_{\sigma,c}\Delta_{\mathsf{id},r\cdot \mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}} \\ &= \Delta_{\sigma,c\sigma\left(r\cdot\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}\right)\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\mathsf{id})}\\ &=\Delta_{\sigma,c\left(r\cdot\sigma\left(\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}\right)\right)\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma, c\left(r\cdot 1\right)}\\ &=\Delta_{\sigma,r\cdot c}. \end{aligned} \] \end{itemize}
For every $\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, $\Delta_{\sigma,1}$ is invertible.
nodes.label: lem:cross-product-delta-invertible

nodes.statement: It is sufficient to prove that $\Delta_{\sigma, 1}$ has a left inverse and right inverse. The left inverse of $\Delta_{\sigma, 1}$ is \[ \Delta_{\sigma^{-1}, \mathfrak{a}\left(\sigma^{-1},\sigma\right)^{-1}\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}. \] Indeed, for any $a \in K$, we have \[ \Delta_{\sigma^{-1}, a}\,\Delta_{\sigma, 1} = \Delta_{\mathsf{id}, a\mathfrak{a}\left(\sigma^{-1},\sigma\right)}, \] hence substitute $a = \mathfrak{a}\left(\sigma^{-1},\sigma\right)^{-1}\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}$, we see the right hand side is $\Delta_{ \mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}$ which is precisely $1 \in \mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$. The right inverse is \[ \Delta_{\sigma^{-1}, \sigma^{-1}\left(\mathfrak{a}\left(\sigma,\sigma^{-1}\right)^{-1} \mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}\right)}. \] Indeed, for any $a \in K$, we have \[ \Delta_{\sigma,1}\,\Delta_{\sigma^{-1},a} = \Delta_{\mathsf{id}, \sigma(a)\mathfrak{a}\left(\sigma,\sigma^{-1}\right)}, \] hence substitude $a = \sigma^{-1}\left(\mathfrak{a}\left(\sigma,\sigma^{-1}\right)^{-1}\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}\right)$, the right hand side is again $\Delta_{\mathsf{id},\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}$ which is precisely $1 \in \mathfrak{C}_{a}$.

For any $c \in K$, we have \[ \Delta_{\sigma,1}\,\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(c) = \iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(\sigma\cdot c)\Delta_{\sigma, 1} = \Delta_{\sigma,\sigma\cdot c} \] and consequently, \[ \Delta_{\sigma,1}\,\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(c)\,\Delta_{\sigma, 1}^{-1} = \iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(\sigma \cdot c). \]
nodes.label: lem:cross-product-basis-conj

nodes.statement: We calculate \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta_{\sigma,1}\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(c) &= \Delta_{\sigma,1}\,\Delta_{\mathsf{id},c\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1}}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma, \sigma(c\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id})^{-1})\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,1)}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma,\sigma(c)\sigma(\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id}))^{-1}\sigma(\mathfrak{a}(\mathsf{id},\mathsf{id}))}\\ &= \Delta_{\sigma,\sigma(c)}. \end{aligned} \]

We have $\Delta_{\sigma,1}\,\Delta_{\tau,1} = \iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau))\Delta_{\sigma\tau,1} = \mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau)\cdot\Delta_{\sigma\tau,1}$ Consequently we have for any $c, d \in K$, \[ \Delta_{\sigma, c}\Delta_{\tau,d} = \left(c \sigma(d)\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau)\right) \cdot \Delta_{\sigma\tau, 1}. \]
nodes.label: lem:cross-product-basis-mul

nodes.statement: The first equality is in~\cref{con:cross-product-iota}. For the second equality, by~\cref{lem:cross-product-basis-conj}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} \Delta_{\sigma,c}\Delta_{\sigma,d} &= \left(c\cdot\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right)\left(d\cdot\Delta_{\tau,1}\right) \\ &= \iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(c)\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(d)\right)\Delta_{\tau, 1} \\ &= \iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\Delta_{\sigma, \sigma \cdot d}\Delta_{\tau, 1}\\ &= c \cdot \sigma(d) \cdot \Delta_{\sigma, 1}\Delta_{\tau, 1} \\ &= c \cdot \sigma(d)\cdot\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau)\cdot\Delta_{\sigma\tau,1}.\\ \end{aligned} \]
The set $\{\Delta_{\sigma, 1}|\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ forms a $K$-basis for $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$.
nodes.label: lem:cross-product-basis

nodes.statement: Suppose some linear combination $\sum_{\sigma}\lambda_{\sigma}\cdot\Delta_{\sigma, 1}$ is $0$ for some $\lambda_{\sigma}$'s in $K$. We have, by the equality in~\cref{con:cross-product-iota} \[ \sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}\lambda_{\sigma}\cdot\Delta_{\sigma,1} = \sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}\Delta_{\sigma,\lambda_{\sigma}} = 0.\\ \] Thus, for any $\tau \in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, we have \[ \left(\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}\lambda_{\sigma}\cdot \Delta_{\sigma,1}\right)(\tau) = 0 = \lambda_{\tau}, \] which proves linear independence. The fact that $\{\Delta_{\sigma, 1}|\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ spans $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ is easy to see because every $\Delta_{\tau, a} = a \cdot \Delta_{\tau, 1}$ is certainly in the span.

When $K/F$ is a finite dimensional Galois extension, the $K$-dimension of $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ is $\dim_{F}K$ and the $F$-dimension of $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ is ${\left(\dim_{F}K\right)}^{2}$.
nodes.label: cor:dim-cross-product

nodes.name: Centrality
nodes.statement: $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ is a central $F$-algebra.
nodes.label: thm:cross-product-central

We see that, for any $\tau \in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, we have \[ z = \sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)} \lambda_{\tau^{-1}\sigma\tau}\cdot\Delta_{\tau^{-1}\sigma\tau,1}. \] Therefore for any $d \in K$ and $\tau\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$, by~\cref{lem:cross-product-basis-mul} and~\cref{lem:cross-product-basis-conj}, we have \[ \begin{aligned} z\, \Delta_{\tau,d} &= \Delta_{\sigma\tau, 1}\\ &= \sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}\left(\lambda_{\sigma}\sigma(d)\mathfrak{a}(\sigma,\tau)\right)\cdot \Delta_{\sigma\tau,1}\\ \Delta_{\tau,d}\, z &= \Delta_{\tau,1}\Delta_{\tau^{-1}\sigma\tau, 1}\\ &= \sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}d\cdot \tau\left(\lambda_{\tau^{-1}\sigma\tau}\right)\cdot \mathfrak{a}\left(\tau,\tau^{-1}\sigma\tau\right)\cdot \Delta_{\sigma\tau, 1}\\ &= \sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)}\left(d\tau\left(\lambda_{\tau^{-1}\sigma\tau}\right)\mathfrak{a}\left(\tau,\tau^{-1}\sigma\tau\right)\right) \cdot \Delta_{\sigma\tau,1}. If $I \ne \mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$, the set $\{\pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right)|\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ forms a $K$-basis for ${}^{\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}}/_{I}$.
nodes.label: lem:cross-product-quotient-basis

nodes.statement: It is easy to see that the set spans ${}^{\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}}/_{I}$ because $\{\Delta_{\sigma, 1}|\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ spans $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ (\cref{lem:cross-product-basis}). For linear-independence, the idea is the same as in the proof of~\cref{thm:conj-seq-basis}. We repeat the argument here. Suppose that $\{\pi\left(\Delta_{sigma, 1}\right)|\sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ is linearly dependent. Let $J \subseteq \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ be such that $\{\pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right)|\sigma\in J\}$ is the maximally linearly independent set. Let $\sigma$ be an arbitrary automorphism that is not in $J$. Therefore, we have $\pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right) \in \left\langle \pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right) | \tau\in J \right\rangle$. Hence we have, by~\cref{con:cross-product-simple-ring-mod} and~\cref{con:cross-product-iota} \[ \pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma,1}\right) = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\lambda_{\tau}\cdot\pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right) = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)\right)\pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right) = \sum_{\tau\in J'}\pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)\Delta_{\tau,1}\right) =\sum_{\tau\in J'}\pi\left(\lambda_{\tau}\cdot \Delta_{\tau, 1}\right). \] for some non-zero $\lambda_{\tau} \in K$ and some $J' \subseteq J$. Hence, for any $c \in K$, we have \[ \begin{aligned} \pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\sigma \cdot c\right)\right) \pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right) &= \pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right)\pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(c)\right) &\text{by~\cref{lem:cross-product-basis-conj}} \\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J} \pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)\right) \pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right) \pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(c)\right)\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J} \pi\left( \iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)\Delta_{\tau, 1} \iota_{\mathfrak{a}} c \right) \\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J} \pi\left( \iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(\tau\cdot c)\Delta_{\tau, 1} \right) & \text{by~\cref{lem:cross-product-basis-conj} again}\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J} \pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c)\right)\right) \pi\left(\Delta_{\tau,1}\right)\\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J} \left(\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c)\right)\cdot \pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right)\\ \pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\sigma \cdot c\right)\right) \pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right) &= \sum_{\tau\in J} \pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}(\sigma\cdot c)\right) \pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\lambda_{\tau}\right)\right) \pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right) \\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J} \pi\left(\iota_{\mathfrak{a}}\left(\sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau}\right)\right) \pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right) \\ &= \sum_{\tau\in J} \left(\sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau}\right)\cdot \pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right). \end{aligned} \] Since, $\{\pi\left(\Delta_{\tau, 1}\right) | \tau \in J\}$ is linearly independent, for all $c \in K$ and $\tau\in J$, we have that $\lambda_{\tau}\tau(c) = \sigma(c)\lambda_{\tau}$. Note that $J' \ne \emptyset$, otherwise, $\pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right) = 0$ implying that $\Delta_{\sigma, 1} \in I$ which by~\cref{lem:cross-product-delta-invertible} is invertible but $I$ does not equal to $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$. Hence for each $\tau \in J'$, we have that for all $c \in K$, since $\lambda_{\tau}$ is not zero, $\sigma(c) = \tau(c)$, i.e. $\sigma = \tau$. Therefore, $\sigma$ is in $J' \subseteq J$ after all.

If $I \ne \mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$, the quotient ring ${}^{\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}}/_{I}$ is isomorphic to $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ as $K$-modules. In particular $\pi$ is a $K$-linear isomorphism between $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ and the quotient ring ${}^{\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}}/_{I}$.

nodes.statement: Indeed, by~\cref{lem:cross-product-basis}, $\{\Delta_{\sigma, 1}|\sigma \in \mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ is a $K$-basis for $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$; and by~\cref{lem:cross-product-quotient-basis}, $\{\pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right) | \sigma\in\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)\}$ is a $K$-basis for ${}^{\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}}/_{I}$. The two sets obviously biject. Hence we can define a $K$-linear isomorphism by $\Delta_{\sigma, 1} \mapsto \pi\left(\Delta_{\sigma, 1}\right)$. This isomorphism is equal to $\pi$ everywhere.

nodes.name: Simple Ring
nodes.statement: $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$ is a simple ring.
nodes.label: cor:cross-product-simple

nodes.statement: For any two-sided-ideal $I$ that is not equal to $\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}$, by~\cref{cor:cross-product-quot-iso}, $\pi : cross_{\mathfrak{a}} \to {}^{\mathfrak{C}_{\mathfrak{a}}}/_{I}$ is a $K$-linear isomorphism, therefore $I$ is equal to $0$.

Let $K/F$ be a finite dimensional and Galois field extension and $\mathfrak{a}$ be a 2-cocycle in $\mathcal{B}^{2}\left(\mathrm{Gal}(K/F), K^{\star}\right)$, $\mathfrak{C}_{a}$ is a finite dimensional central simple $F$-algebra.
